reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: Suspect PHACE in any infant with a large (typically >5 cm) segmental infantile haemangioma of the face, scalp or neck rather than a small focal lesion

The acronym captures Posterior fossa brain malformations, Haemangioma, Arterial cerebrovascular anomalies, Cardiac defects (notably coarctation of the aorta) and Eye abnormalities; ventral developmental defects (sternal cleft, supraumbilical raphe) extend it to PHACE(S)
Facial haemangiomas follow recognised segmental patterns, and frontotemporal or mandibular segments carry the highest association with extracutaneous anomalies
Cerebral and cervical arterial anomalies (dysplasia, aberrant origin, stenosis, absence) predispose to acute ischaemic stroke and are a leading cause of morbidity
As an infantile haemangioma, the cutaneous lesion is GLUT1-positive and follows the proliferate-then-involute course of true vascular tumours in the ISSVA framework
Airway (subglottic) haemangioma should be considered when a beard-distribution segmental lesion is present with stridor
Baseline MRI/MRA of the brain, head and neck, echocardiography with aortic arch imaging, and ophthalmology and cardiology review are the core evaluation
Beta-blocker therapy (propranolol for infantile-haemangioma-type lesions) is first-line for the haemangioma but is used cautiously given the risk of arteriopathy and coarctation
reference.pathophysiology: PHACE is a neurocutaneous condition in which a large segmental infantile haemangioma occurs together with malformations of structures that share regional embryonic development, particularly the cephalic neural crest and cranial vasculature. The haemangioma itself is a benign GLUT1-positive vascular tumour of proliferating endothelium. The associated arterial, posterior fossa, cardiac, ocular and ventral midline anomalies are thought to reflect a field defect arising during early fetal development of the head and upper thorax; the cause is not fully understood, most cases are sporadic, and a striking female predominance is observed.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated segmental infantile haemangioma without extracutaneous involvement
Congenital haemangioma (rapidly involuting or non-involuting, GLUT1-negative)
Sturge-Weber syndrome (capillary malformation in a trigeminal distribution)
LUMBAR/PELVIS syndrome (segmental haemangioma of the lower body)
Capillary malformation of a port-wine type
additionalInvestigations: MRI and MRA of the brain, head and neck to define posterior fossa and cerebrovascular anomalies
Echocardiography with dedicated imaging of the aortic arch to detect coarctation and arch anomalies
Detailed ophthalmological examination for posterior segment and optic anomalies
Clinical examination of the sternum and abdomen for ventral midline defects
Laryngoscopy or airway assessment when a beard-distribution lesion or stridor is present
Developmental and neurological follow-up including hearing assessment
redFlags: Acute focal neurological deficit suggesting arterial ischaemic stroke from cerebral arteriopathy
Signs of aortic coarctation or heart failure requiring urgent cardiology input
Stridor or respiratory distress indicating airway haemangioma
Progressive visual compromise from orbital or posterior segment involvement
Feeding or swallowing difficulty and failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous haemangioma usually proliferates then involutes, but long-term outcome is dominated by the extracutaneous anomalies; cerebral arteriopathy carries a lifelong stroke risk, and cardiac, ocular and neurodevelopmental problems may cause lasting morbidity. Coordinated multidisciplinary surveillance is essential.
pitfalls: Treating a large segmental facial haemangioma as isolated and omitting brain, arch and eye imaging
Starting beta-blocker therapy without first excluding significant arteriopathy or coarctation that alters cerebral perfusion
Attributing later neurological events solely to the haemangioma rather than the underlying arteriopathy
Overlooking subtle ventral midline defects that complete the PHACES spectrum
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Oral propranolol as first-line therapy for the segmental infantile haemangioma, started cautiously after cardiac and cerebrovascular assessment given the arterial anomaly and stroke risk
Baseline MRI and MRA of the brain, head and neck with echocardiography and dedicated aortic arch imaging to define associated anomalies before treatment
Stroke-risk mitigation for cerebral arteriopathy with careful blood-pressure and perfusion management and avoidance of abrupt haemodynamic change
Airway management for subglottic beard-distribution haemangioma causing stridor, using systemic therapy and airway intervention as needed
Ophthalmology-directed treatment with corneal and visual protection for ocular involvement
Cardiology management of coarctation and arch anomalies, including surgical repair where indicated
Long-term neurodevelopmental and hearing follow-up coordinated across dermatology, neurology, cardiology and ophthalmology
